title: Of conscience
paragraphs: The Sieur de la Brousse, my brother, and I, travelling one day together during the time of our civil wars, met a gentleman of good standing. He was of the opposite party, though I did not know it, for he pretended otherwise. The trouble in this kind of war is that the cards are so shuffled — your enemy not distinguished from yourself by any obvious mark of language or dress, having been raised under the same laws, climate, and manners — that it is very hard to avoid confusion and disorder. This made me afraid of meeting any of our own troops in a place where I was not known, that I might not be in fear to tell my name, and perhaps worse — as had happened to me before, when by such a mistake I lost both men and horses, including an Italian gentleman, my page, whom I had bred with the greatest care and affection, in whom a youth of great promise was wretchedly extinguished. But the gentleman my brother and I met had so desperate, half-dead a fear of meeting any horsemen or passing by any of the towns that held for the King, that I at last realised it was the alarm of conscience. The poor man felt as if through his visor and the crosses on his cassock one might have seen into his bosom and read the most secret intentions of his heart — so wonderful is the power of conscience. It makes us betray, accuse, and fight against ourselves, and for want of other witnesses, give evidence against ourselves:
"Occultum quatiens animo tortore flagellum."
["The torturer of the soul brandishing a hidden lash within." — Juvenal, iii. 195.]

This story is in every child's mouth: Bessus the Paeonian, reproached for wantonly pulling down a nest of young sparrows and killing them, replied that he had reason to do so, since those little birds never ceased falsely accusing him of the murder of his father. The parricide had until then been concealed and unknown, but the avenging fury of conscience caused it to be revealed by the very man who was to suffer for it. Hesiod corrects Plato's saying that punishment closely follows sin: it is, he says, born at the same moment as the sin. Whoever expects punishment already suffers it, and whoever has deserved it expects it. Wickedness contrives torments against itself:
"Malum consilium consultori pessimum."
["Bad counsel is worst for the counsellor." — in Aulus Gellius, iv. 5.]
— as the wasp stings and hurts another but most of all itself, since it loses its sting and its use forever there:
"Vitasque in vulnere ponunt."
["And leave their own lives in the wound." — Virgil, Georg., iv. 238.]

The cantharides carry about them, by a quirk of nature, an antidote to their own poison. In the same way, at the very moment when men take delight in vice, there springs in the conscience a discomfort that torments us sleeping and waking with various distressing fancies:
"Quippe ubi se multi, per somnia saepe loquentes, Aut morbo delirantes, protraxe ferantur, Et celata diu in medium peccata dedisse."
["Surely many men, often talking in their sleep or raving in disease, are said to have betrayed themselves and brought to light offences long concealed." — Lucretius, v. 1157.]

Apollodorus dreamed that he saw himself flayed by the Scythians and then boiled in a cauldron, and that his heart muttered these words: "I am the cause of all these miseries that have come on you." Epicurus said that no hiding-place could conceal the wicked, since they could never be sure of being hidden while their conscience exposed them to themselves.
"Prima est haec ultio, quod se Judice nemo nocens absolvitur."
["This is the first punishment of guilt: that no guilty man is acquitted in his own court." — Juvenal, xiii. 2.]

As a bad conscience fills us with fear, so a good one gives us greater confidence and assurance; and I can truly say that I have gone through several dangers with a steadier step because of the secret knowledge I had of my own will and the innocence of my intentions:
"Conscia mens ut cuique sua est, ita concipit intra Pectora pro facto spemque metumque suo."
["As each man's conscience is, so within his breast he conceives hope or fear, according to his deed." — Ovid, Fast., i. 485.]

There are a thousand examples of this; but three of one and the same person will be enough. Scipio, being accused one day before the people of Rome of crimes of a very high nature, instead of excusing himself or flattering his judges, said, "It will be a fine thing for you to sit in judgment on a head by whose means you have the power to judge all the world." Another time, to a string of impeachments brought against him by a tribune of the people, instead of making his defence he said, "Let us go, citizens — let us go and give thanks to the gods for the victory they gave me over the Carthaginians on this day," and walking off ahead toward the temple, he had presently the whole assembly, and his accuser himself, following at his heels. And when Petilius, put up to it by Cato, demanded an account of the money that had passed through his hands in the province of Antioch, Scipio, coming into the senate for that purpose, produced from under his robe a book in which, he told them, was an exact account of his receipts and disbursements; but when he was asked to hand it over to the prothonotary for examination, he refused, saying he would not do himself so great a disgrace, and in the presence of the whole senate tore the book in pieces with his own hands. I do not believe that the most calloused conscience could have counterfeited so great an assurance. He had naturally too high a spirit and was used to too high a fortune, says Titus Livius, to know how to be guilty, and to lower himself to the meanness of defending his innocence. The putting of men to the rack is a dangerous invention, and seems to be more a trial of patience than of truth. Both the man who has the fortitude to endure it conceals the truth, and the man who has not — for why should pain sooner make me confess what is, than force me to say what is not? And on the other hand, if the man who is not guilty of what he is accused of has the courage to undergo those torments, why should not the guilty man have the same, when so fair a reward as life is in his sights? I believe the basis of this invention comes from considering the force of conscience: for in the guilty man it seems to assist the rack in making him confess his fault and shake his resolution; and in the innocent it fortifies him against the torture. But, all said, it is in plain truth a trial full of uncertainty and danger. What would not a man say, what would not a man do, to avoid such unbearable torments?
"Etiam innocentes cogit mentiri dolor."
["Pain will make even the innocent lie." — Publius Syrus, De Dolore.]

From which it comes that he whom the judge has racked in order not to put him to death innocent, ends by being put to death both innocent and racked. A thousand and a thousand have charged their own heads by false confessions — among whom I count Philotas, considering the circumstances of the trial Alexander put him to and the course of his torture. But, so it goes, some say it is the least evil human weakness could invent. Very inhumanly, even so, and to very little purpose, in my opinion.

Many nations, less barbarous in this than the Greeks and Romans who call them so, hold it horrible and cruel to torment and tear a man to pieces for a fault of which they are still in doubt. How can he help your ignorance? Are you not unjust who, to avoid killing him without cause, do worse than kill him? And to prove this, just observe how often men prefer to die without reason rather than undergo this examination, more painful than the execution itself, and which often anticipates execution by its very extremity and carries it out. I do not know where I got this story, but it exactly matches the conscience of our justice in this regard. A countrywoman accused, before a general of very severe discipline, one of his soldiers of having taken from her children the little bit of broth she had left to feed them with, the army having consumed all the rest; but there was no proof of it. The general, having warned the woman to be very careful what she said, for that she would make herself guilty of a false accusation if she lied, and she sticking to her story, he at once had the soldier's belly slit open to find out the truth of the fact — and the woman was found to be right. An instructive sentence.
